claims.text: The tribo-corrosion degradation of CoCrFeMnNi is governed by the balance between mechanical passive-film removal and electrochemical repassivation.
When repassivation sufficiently compensates for wear-induced film loss, the passive film remains effective and reduces corrosion and total material loss.
The proposed specimens are highly polished, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloys.
In-situ EC-AFM will be used during simultaneous sliding and corrosion testing to monitor oxide-film thickness and morphology.
Testing is proposed in 3.5 wt% NaCl at fixed potential and constant normal load, sliding speed, and sliding distance.
Moderate wear rates will permit observable passive-film dynamics.
Mechanical wear continuously thins the protective oxide layer.
Electrochemical processes repassivate surfaces exposed by mechanical wear.
The net balance of removal and repassivation rates determines whether the passive film retains integrity and shields the alloy from corrosive attack.
Moderate wear with sufficiently rapid repassivation will produce cyclic thinning and regrowth of the passive film.
Such moderate-wear conditions will produce lower corrosion rates and less total degradation than conditions in which film removal outpaces repassivation.
Excessive wear intensity will diminish passive-film protection and accelerate degradation.
The proposed baseline is the same alloy with minimal mechanical perturbation or in a well-established passive state.
The prediction should hold when wear is moderate and the potential and electrolyte permit noticeable repassivation.
The prediction may fail under extreme wear or at potentials that inhibit repassivation or destabilize passive films.
Available literature supports the proposed repassivation mechanism.
The quantitative balance between repassivation and removal and its sensitivity to sliding conditions remain experimentally undetermined.
A lack of correlated film-thickness recovery, repassivation response, corrosion rate, and total degradation across wear intensities would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
